cards.title: Before we start: from 'Wo ist die Seilbahn?' to 'Können Sie mir sagen, wo die Seilbahn abfährt?'
cards.body: Mira is in Innsbruck and needs facts: when does the cable car go, what does it cost, where is the viewpoint? At the tourist office she asks politely and later tells Leon what she heard. You know all the tools already: indirect questions from A2 and dass-clauses from lesson 4. Today you use them together.
steps: You already know: Wann fährt der Bus? and Weißt du, ob der Bus um acht fährt? (indirect questions, A2 chapter 7).
New today: no new rule, but a new situation: polite questions to a stranger with Sie, and passing the answer on with dass.
By the end you can: get information at a tourist office and report it to a friend.

examples.de: Wann fährt der Bus?
examples.en: When does the bus leave?
examples.why: You know this already: a direct question.

examples.de: Weißt du, ob der Bus um acht fährt?
examples.en: Do you know if the bus leaves at eight?
examples.why: You know this too: an indirect question, the verb is last.

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wo die Seilbahn abfährt?
examples.en: Can you tell me where the cable car leaves from?
examples.why: New today: the same pattern, but polite, with Sie, at the tourist office.

cards.more: Imagine asking a stranger for the time. You would not shout Wie spät? You would say Entschuldigung, wissen Sie, wie spät es ist? The polite wrapper makes your question softer, and German builds it with the same trick you know: the wrapper comes first, then the question word, and the verb jumps to the end. In this lesson we use that trick in a real place, the Touristeninformation, and then we pass on what we learned.

cards.title: At the Touristeninformation
cards.body: A Touristeninformation gives you maps, tips and tickets. Open with Ich möchte mich nach … erkundigen (I would like to ask about …). Then ask for material: Haben Sie einen Prospekt über …? Or ask about a discount: Gibt es eine Gästekarte? Always use Sie and end with a thank you.
cards.lead: Mira stands at the counter. First we learn how such a talk goes and the phrases you need to start it politely and to ask for brochures and the guest card.

examples.de: Guten Tag, ich möchte mich nach Führungen erkundigen.
examples.en: Hello, I would like to ask about guided tours.

examples.de: Haben Sie einen Prospekt über Innsbruck?
examples.en: Do you have a brochure about Innsbruck?

examples.de: Gibt es eine Gästekarte?
examples.en: Is there a guest card?

examples.de: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe!
examples.en: Thank you very much for your help!

deeper.text: sich erkundigen nach + dative is the formal cousin of fragen nach. You hear it at counters, on the phone and in emails. The little sich changes with the person: ich erkundige mich, Sie erkundigen sich, Mira erkundigt sich. The topic always follows nach in the dative: nach dem Preis, nach der Anfahrt, nach Führungen. Learn it as one chunk with its three parts.

example.de: Ich erkundige mich nach dem Preis.
example.en: I am enquiring about the price.

cards.more: Picture a small shop counter with four stations. At station one you say hello. At station two you say what you want to know: Ich möchte mich nach … erkundigen. At station three you ask for something to take away, a Prospekt or a Gästekarte. At station four you say thank you and leave. Each station has one sentence, and the whole talk takes less than a minute. Walk the four stations in your head before you speak.
steps: 1 Greet: Guten Tag!
2 Say your topic: Ich möchte mich nach … erkundigen.
3 Ask follow-up questions: Haben Sie …? Gibt es …?
4 Thank them: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe!

cards.title: Polite questions: the verb goes last
cards.body: A polite question has two parts: a wrapper (Können Sie mir sagen, … or Wissen Sie, …) and the question inside. The question word stays, the verb goes to the end. For yes/no questions there is no question word, so use ob. Compare: Gibt es eine Gästekarte? / … ob es eine Gästekarte gibt.
cards.lead: You know the pattern from A2. Here we put it into one table, so you can see how a direct question turns into a polite one for the tourist office.

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wann die Seilbahn fährt?
examples.en: Can you tell me when the cable car runs?

examples.de: Wissen Sie, wo der Wanderweg ist?
examples.en: Do you know where the hiking trail is?

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wie viel die Rundfahrt kostet?
examples.en: Can you tell me how much the tour costs?

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, ob es eine Gästekarte gibt?
examples.en: Can you tell me whether there is a guest card?

deeper.text: Notice the punctuation. If the wrapper is a question (Können Sie mir sagen, …?), the whole sentence ends with a question mark, even though the inner part is not a question. If the wrapper is a statement (Ich weiß nicht, …), the sentence ends with a full stop. The inner question word never gets its own question mark. This is how you recognise whether an indirect sentence is asking or telling.

example.de: Ich weiß nicht, wann die Seilbahn fährt.
example.en: I don't know when the cable car runs.

cards.more: Think of a gift. The direct question Wann fährt die Seilbahn? is the gift without wrapping: honest but a bit bare. The wrapper Können Sie mir sagen, … is the wrapping paper. You put the question word and the content inside, and the verb goes to the bottom of the box, to the very end. For yes/no questions the box needs a label: ob. Wrap your questions in German, and strangers will smile at you.

cards.title: Understanding the answer
cards.body: Answers at a tourist office contain four kinds of facts: time, price, place and condition. Listen for key words: von … bis, um … Uhr, kostet, pro Person, kostenlos, am Ausgangspunkt and wenn. You do not need every word. Catch the key words and you understand the answer.
cards.lead: Now the other side of the counter: you must understand what the employee says. This card shows the four kinds of facts you will hear and the key words that signal each of them.

examples.de: Die Seilbahn fährt von Juni bis Oktober.
examples.en: The cable car runs from June to October.

examples.de: Eine Rundfahrt kostet 18 Euro pro Person.
examples.en: A tour costs 18 euros per person.

examples.de: Der Ausgangspunkt für die Wanderung ist hinter dem Bahnhof.
examples.en: The starting point for the hike is behind the station.

examples.de: Wenn Sie eine Gästekarte haben, ist die Seilbahn kostenlos.
examples.en: If you have a guest card, the cable car is free of charge.

deeper.text: In many German and Austrian holiday regions, the hotel gives you a Gästekarte at check-in. It often includes local buses or cable cars, for free or at a lower price. What exactly is included depends on the region, so it is smart to ask: Was ist mit der Gästekarte inklusive? That one question can save you a lot of money on holiday.

example.de: Mit der Gästekarte fahren Sie kostenlos mit dem Bus.
example.en: With the guest card you ride the bus free of charge.

cards.more: Imagine four coloured highlighters. Yellow for time, green for price, blue for place, orange for conditions. While the employee talks, you mentally highlight the key words: von Juni bis Oktober is yellow, 18 Euro pro Person is green, hinter dem Bahnhof is blue, wenn Sie eine Gästekarte haben is orange. You do not need to catch every word. If you have all four colours, you have the full answer and can act on it.

cards.title: Passing it on with dass and da
cards.body: Later you tell a friend what you heard. Use dass: Die Frau hat gesagt, dass die Rundfahrt um 10 Uhr beginnt. The verb of the dass-clause goes last. To explain what you do because of it, add da or weil: Da die Seilbahn nur bis 17 Uhr fährt, gehen wir früh los.
cards.lead: You now have the facts. This card shows how to pass them on to someone else with dass and how to use da and weil for what follows from them.

examples.de: Die Frau hat gesagt, dass die Rundfahrt um 10 Uhr beginnt.
examples.en: The woman said that the tour begins at 10 o'clock.

examples.de: Die Frau sagt, dass die Seilbahn mit der Gästekarte kostenlos ist.
examples.en: The woman says that the cable car is free with the guest card.

examples.de: Da die Seilbahn nur bis 17 Uhr fährt, gehen wir früh los.
examples.en: Since the cable car only runs until 5 pm, we set off early.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass die Rundfahrt eine Stunde dauert.
examples.en: I think the tour takes an hour.

deeper.text: English shifts the tense when it reports: She said that the tour began at 10. German keeps the present: Sie hat gesagt, dass die Rundfahrt um 10 Uhr beginnt. You say it the way it is true now, and nobody misunderstands you. So you only need the present tense and dass to pass on information, which makes German easier here than English.

example.de: Mira schreibt, dass sie morgen wandert.
example.en: Mira writes that she is going hiking tomorrow.

cards.more: Think of a messenger carrying a note. The note says: Die Rundfahrt beginnt um 10 Uhr. The messenger does not change the words, he just puts the note into a small envelope: Die Frau hat gesagt, dass … The envelope is the word dass, and the verb of the note moves to the bottom. That is all. The note keeps its present tense. When you tell Leon, you hand him the note in its envelope.

Die Seilbahn ist mit der Gästekarte kostenlos.

cards.title: Mira in Innsbruck: the talk
cards.body: Mira visits the Touristeninformation in Innsbruck and speaks Sie. Listen for the four facts: time, price, place, condition. Notice which polite questions she uses and how the employee answers with wenn and weil. Read the talk twice: first for meaning, then to find every verb at the end.
cards.lead: Now everything comes together in one talk: the greeting, polite questions, the answers with wenn and weil, and a recommendation at the end.

examples.en: Mira: Hello! I would like to ask about hikes.

examples.en: Mira: Can you tell me where the viewpoint is?

examples.de: Er ist oben, direkt an der Seilbahn. Von dort sehen Sie die ganze Stadt.

examples.de: Danke! Was können Sie mir empfehlen?

examples.en: Employee: I recommend the tour to you because you see a lot of the city on it.

deeper.text: Staff at tourist offices often answer in short pieces: Gern. Bitte schön. Oben. Hinter dem Bahnhof. In spoken German a fragment is a complete answer, and you can do the same. If someone asks Wo ist der Aussichtspunkt? you can simply say Oben. Full sentences are for the questions. Short answers make you sound natural, and they are easier to understand.

example.de: Bitte schön, hier ist der Prospekt.
example.en: Here you are, here is the brochure.

cards.more: Think of the talk as a short film with ten scenes. In every scene one person speaks and the other one listens for a key fact. Mira asks, the employee answers, and each answer has one colour: time, price, place or advice. Watch the film twice. The first time you only follow the story. The second time you freeze each scene and underline the verb at the end of every side clause. Then you have watched and practised in one go.
steps: 1 Read once for the story: what does Mira find out?
2 Mark time, price, place and condition.
3 Find the verb at the end of every clause with ob, wo or weil.

cards.title: Role-play: you at the counter
cards.body: Now you are Mira. Four question cards help you play the talk: when, how much, brochure, recommendation. Ask each one with a polite wrapper and answer with a full sentence and a reason if you can. Use Sie with the employee and du with a friend. Practise aloud, not only in your head.
cards.lead: Now it is your turn. This card gives you four question cards for your own role-play, with possible answers, so you can practise asking and answering aloud.

deeper.text: In role plays, expand your answers with a reason. Instead of just Das nehme ich, say Das nehme ich, weil es kostenlos ist. A short reason with weil lifts your German from A2 to B1, and you already know the rule: the verb goes last. In an exam, a reason is often the difference between a short answer and a good answer.

example.en: I'll take that because it is free of charge.

Each card is a small question with a wrapper you know: Können Sie mir sagen, … or Wissen Sie, ob … Draw all four cards twice, once as the visitor with Sie and once as a friend with du. Eight short rounds, and your tongue will remember the verb at the end.

lessons.title: Obwohl es regnet, wandern wir: saying 'although'
lessons.goal: Say that something happens against expectation with obwohl (verb at the end), put the obwohl clause first or second, and compare it with trotzdem and aber.

grammar.point: obwohl names a fact that should stop you but does not. It sends its verb to the end like weil: Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet. If the obwohl clause comes first, the main clause begins with its verb: Obwohl es regnet, wandern wir. Es regnet, trotzdem wandern wir means the same, but trotzdem is followed by the verb at once. Never use obwohl and trotzdem together in one sentence.

mistake.why: The obwohl clause is position 1 of the whole sentence, so the main clause starts with its verb: obwohl-part, comma, verb.

terms.meaning: a word that joins two clauses: weil, obwohl, dass
a clause that starts with a conjunction like weil or obwohl; its verb stands at the end

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Es regnet, trotzdem wandern wir' to 'Obwohl es regnet, wandern wir'
cards.body: Mira and Leon stand at the foot of a mountain in Tirol. Grey clouds, light rain. Mira says: Es regnet, trotzdem wandern wir. You know that from A2. Today you learn a second way to say the same thing. It sounds natural in stories and fits into longer sentences: obwohl.
steps: You already know: Es regnet. Trotzdem wandern wir. And: Wir wandern, weil das Wetter schön ist.
New today: Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet. obwohl means although, and its verb goes to the end of the clause.
By the end you can: say what you do against all odds, use obwohl at the start and in the middle of a sentence, and chat about a day in the mountains.

examples.de: Es regnet. Trotzdem wandern wir.
examples.en: It is raining. Still, we are hiking.
examples.why: You know this: trotzdem, and the verb comes right after it.

examples.de: Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet.
examples.en: We are hiking although it is raining.
examples.why: New today: obwohl sends regnet to the end.

cards.more: Think of a friend who says: I know it is raining, but I am going out anyway. In English you add although to the rain part. German does the same, and then it does one more thing it always does after words like weil: it pushes the verb of that part to the very end. You already do this with weil. obwohl follows the same road, only with the opposite message.

cards.title: weil or obwohl? One rainy day, two plans
cards.body: Look at the weather: Es regnet. What do you expect? You stay inside. Wir bleiben in der Hütte (hut), weil es regnet. weil gives the reason, and the result is what you expect. Now the surprise: Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet. obwohl names something that should stop us, but does not.
cards.lead: Last lesson ended with da and weil, which both give a reason. Now we meet the opposite word: it names something that should stop you, and you do it anyway. One rainy day shows both plans.

examples.de: Wir bleiben in der Hütte, weil es regnet.
examples.en: We stay in the hut because it is raining.

examples.de: Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet.
examples.en: We are hiking although it is raining.

examples.de: Leon schläft lange, weil er müde ist.
examples.en: Leon sleeps long because he is tired.

deeper.text: obwohl always names a real fact. Do not mix it up with wenn. Wir wandern, wenn es regnet means: whenever it rains, we hike (a habit or a condition). Wir wandern, obwohl es regnet means: today it is raining and we hike anyway. wenn can be a maybe, obwohl is a real situation.

example.de: Wir wandern, wenn es regnet.
example.en: We hike whenever it rains.

cards.more: Draw two arrows on paper. The first points from the rain straight to the hut. That is the arrow you expect, and weil follows it: rain, so we stay. Now draw a second arrow that bends away from the rain and climbs up the mountain. That bent arrow is obwohl. Test it in your head: if the sentence sounds like rain, but we go anyway, use obwohl. If it sounds like rain, so we stay, use weil.

rows: Wir bleiben hier, weil es regnet.
obstacle that does not stop us

cards.title: obwohl in the middle: the verb goes to the end
cards.body: obwohl works like weil. Main clause first, comma, obwohl, subject, other words, and the verb at the very end. With Perfekt or a modal verb, both verb parts go to the end, with the conjugated verb last: obwohl sie eine Blase (blister) hat, obwohl wir früh aufgestanden sind, obwohl er eine Pause machen möchte.
cards.lead: Now we look at the clause that starts with obwohl. It has the same shape as a weil clause, so you only have to trust what you already do. We check it with a simple verb, with Perfekt and with a modal.

examples.de: Mira geht weiter, obwohl sie eine Blase hat.
examples.en: Mira keeps going although she has a blister.

examples.de: Wir sind fit, obwohl wir früh aufgestanden sind.
examples.en: We are fit although we got up early.

examples.de: Leon geht weiter, obwohl er eine Pause machen möchte.
examples.en: Leon keeps going although he would like a break.

examples.de: Leon ist glücklich, obwohl er Muskelkater hat.
examples.en: Leon is happy although he has sore muscles.

deeper.text: A separable verb joins up again at the end of an obwohl clause. In a main clause the prefix splits off: Leon steht früh auf. In the obwohl clause it is one word again: obwohl er früh aufsteht. With a modal, the infinitive stays whole before the modal: obwohl er früh aufstehen muss. Learners often write obwohl er steht früh auf. That is wrong.

example.de: Leon lacht, obwohl er früh aufstehen muss.
example.en: Leon laughs although he has to get up early.

cards.more: Imagine the obwohl clause as a corridor. The conjunction opens the door, the subject walks in, then the other words follow, and the verb waits at the last door at the end of the corridor. English keeps the verb near the front: although she has a blister. German makes you walk the whole corridor first. If there are two verbs, they wait together, and the one that changes with the person stands last.
steps: 1 Say the main clause first: Mira geht weiter.
2 Comma, then obwohl.
3 The subject and all other words: sie eine Blase.
4 The verb goes last: hat. (Perfekt or modal: both verbs at the end.)

cards.title: obwohl first: verb, comma, verb
cards.body: The obwohl clause can also open the sentence. Then it counts as the first position of the whole sentence, so the main clause starts with its verb right after the comma. You get two verbs next to the comma: Obwohl der Weg steil ist, gehen wir bis zum Gipfel (summit). Verb at the end, comma, verb.
cards.lead: You can also put the obwohl part first. This is easy to get wrong, because the main clause now begins with the verb. This card shows that rhythm: the verb sits before the comma and again after it.

examples.de: Obwohl der Weg steil ist, gehen wir bis zum Gipfel.
examples.en: Although the path is steep, we walk to the summit.

examples.de: Obwohl Mira eine Blase hat, geht sie weiter.
examples.en: Although Mira has a blister, she keeps going.

examples.de: Obwohl Leon müde ist, trägt er den Rucksack.
examples.en: Although Leon is tired, he carries the rucksack.

deeper.text: Both orders mean the same, but they feel different. With obwohl in the second place the obstacle sounds like an afterthought. With obwohl first the obstacle gets the spotlight, and the reader waits for the surprise. That is why obwohl first is very common in blogs, letters and stories. When you speak, you make a small pause at the comma.

example.de: Obwohl der Aufstieg hart war, war der Blick vom Gipfel großartig.
example.en: Although the climb was hard, the view from the summit was great.

cards.more: Think of a drum roll before a surprise. The obwohl clause is the drum roll: Obwohl der Weg so steil ist … The main clause is the surprise: … gehen wir bis zum Gipfel! Inside the sentence the two verbs stand like two bookends around the comma. If you only see one verb next to the comma, something is missing. Check the second half: it must start with the verb.

cards.title: Two ways, same meaning: obwohl, trotzdem and aber
cards.body: You know trotzdem. Es ist neblig, trotzdem steigen wir auf. means the same as Obwohl es neblig ist, steigen wir auf. The difference is the verb position: after trotzdem the verb follows at once, after obwohl it goes to the end. aber is the simple contrast. It does not change the word order.
cards.lead: Now we put the three contrast words side by side. Two of them say the same thing with different word order, and the third is the simplest. Seeing them together helps you choose the right one fast.

examples.de: Es ist neblig, trotzdem steigen wir auf.
examples.en: It is foggy, still we climb up.

examples.de: Obwohl es neblig ist, steigen wir auf.
examples.en: Although it is foggy, we climb up.

examples.de: Der Aufstieg war anstrengend, aber schön.
examples.en: The climb was hard, but beautiful.

deeper.text: In everyday talk you sometimes hear obwohl alone at the start of a new sentence, as a correction of yourself: Ich komme mit. Obwohl, ich habe keine Zeit. Here the word order after obwohl is normal. This is spoken German only. In writing and in exams, obwohl always sends the verb to the end of its clause.

example.de: Ich komme mit. Obwohl, ich habe keine Zeit.
example.en: I am coming along. Although, I have no time.

cards.more: Think of one key for one lock. A contrast needs only one contrast word. Wrong: Obwohl es regnet, trotzdem wandern wir. Both words try to do the same job, so you have one key too many. Choose one. Obwohl es regnet, wandern wir. Or: Es regnet, trotzdem wandern wir. And aber is the easiest: it joins two parts and the word order does not change at all.

rows: Es ist neblig, trotzdem steigen wir auf.
Wir steigen auf, obwohl es neblig ist.
Der Aufstieg war anstrengend, aber schön.

cards.title: Hiking safety: weil and obwohl on the mountain
cards.body: In the mountains the weather decides. Check the Wettervorhersage (weather forecast) before you start. If a Gewitter comes, you turn back: umkehren. Now use both words: Wir sind umgekehrt, weil ein Gewitter gekommen ist. Obwohl die Wettervorhersage gut war, hat es geregnet. Good boots matter too: the path can be rutschig (slippery).
cards.lead: Here the new word meets real mountain life. You practise weil for a reason to stop and obwohl for something that went against your plan, with the forecast, the path and a thunderstorm.

examples.de: Wir sind umgekehrt, weil ein Gewitter gekommen ist.
examples.en: We turned back because a thunderstorm came.

examples.de: Obwohl die Wettervorhersage gut war, hat es geregnet.
examples.en: Although the forecast was good, it rained.

examples.de: Wir gehen nicht weiter, weil der Weg rutschig ist.
examples.en: We do not go on because the path is slippery.

deeper.text: umkehren is separable (er kehrt um) and makes its Perfekt with sein, because you move: Wir sind umgekehrt. Culture tip: in the Alps, thunderstorms often build up in the afternoon. So hikers start early and aim to be back at the hut by lunch. Turning back is never a shame, it is the normal, clever thing to do.

example.de: Wir sind umgekehrt, obwohl der Gipfel nah war.
example.en: We turned back although the summit was near.

cards.more: Think of a traffic light in the sky. Green sky and a good forecast: go on. Yellow clouds: look at the clock and at the path. Red and black sky: umkehren. weil explains why you stop. obwohl explains why you went on, or why the day was different from the plan. Careful hikers say weil often, stubborn ones say obwohl a lot. Both words are useful when you tell the story afterwards.
steps: 1 Look at the Wettervorhersage the evening before.
2 Start early: Gewitter often come in the afternoon.
3 Wear good Wanderschuhe, because the path can be rutschig.
4 If the sky gets dark: umkehren. No summit is worth the risk.

cards.title: On the trail: Mira and Leon decide
cards.body: Read the short trail dialogue. Mira and Leon climb in the fog, Mira has a blister, and they must decide: go on or turn back? Watch how obwohl, trotzdem and weil carry the conversation. Two chunks help in a bad moment: Halb so schlimm. (not that bad) and Wir schaffen das! (we can do it).
cards.lead: Now everything comes together in a real conversation. Read it once for the story, then again to find every obwohl, trotzdem and weil, and the two useful phrases for a hard day.

examples.de: Der Nebel ist dick, aber wir steigen weiter auf.
examples.en: The fog is thick, but we are climbing on.

examples.de: Halb so schlimm. Wir schaffen das!
examples.en: Not that bad. We can do it!

examples.de: Mira geht weiter, obwohl sie müde ist.
examples.en: Mira keeps going although she is tired.

deeper.text: schaffen has two meanings. Wir schaffen das! means we can do it, we will manage it. Wir haben den Gipfel geschafft means we reached it. Together they make a nice chunk for an encouraging friend: Du schaffst das! Halb so schlimm is also a way to calm someone down after a small problem, for example a mistake or a lost minute.

example.de: Du schaffst das!
example.en: You can do it!

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a small play. Two friends, one decision. Mira does not want to stop, Leon worries about the blister, and in the end the sun decides. Underline every verb at the end of a clause, and write down the sentences that start with obwohl. Then cover the German and say them from the English. After the second reading the order stops feeling strange.
steps: Leon: Der Nebel wird immer dicker. Sollen wir umkehren?
Mira: Nein, noch nicht. Obwohl es neblig ist, sehen wir den Weg gut.
Leon: Du gehst so langsam. Hast du eine Blase?
Mira: Ja, weil die Wanderschuhe neu sind. Halb so schlimm, ich gehe weiter.
Leon: Gut, aber wir machen eine Pause. Es ist rutschig, deshalb gehen wir langsam.
Mira: Einverstanden. Obwohl ich müde bin, möchte ich zum Gipfel.
Leon: Wir sind schon sehr hoch. Hast du noch Wasser?
Mira: Ja, hier. Und siehst du? Der Nebel geht weg. Wir schaffen das!

lessons.title: Das war ein Urlaub!: telling a holiday story
lessons.goal: Tell what happened on a holiday, with good and bad moments, in Perfekt with als, weil, da and obwohl, and end with your opinion.

grammar.topic: Telling a holiday story in the Perfekt
grammar.point: A story has steps: when and where, start (zuerst, dann), problem (plötzlich, leider), rescue (zum Glück), end (am Ende). Use the Perfekt for actions and war or hatte for states. In side clauses with als, weil, da, obwohl the verb parts go to the end: Als wir angekommen sind, hat es geregnet. No new grammar, just use.
grammar.oneLine: Obwohl wir den Anschluss verpasst haben, war es ein unvergesslicher Urlaub.

mistake.wrong: Als wir sind angekommen, hat es geregnet.
mistake.right: Als wir angekommen sind, hat es geregnet.
mistake.why: After als the whole verb group goes to the end, and the finite verb sind stands last.

terms.meaning: the spoken past: haben or sein + participle at the end
the verb that changes with the person, like sind or hat

cards.title: Before we start: from single sentences to a holiday story
cards.body: After a holiday everybody asks: Wie war's? A good answer is not one sentence, it is a small story with a beginning, a problem and an ending. You already have all the grammar for it. Today you put the pieces together, and add the little words that make a story feel alive.
steps: You already know: Wir sind nach Tirol gefahren. Als wir angekommen sind, hat es geregnet.
New today: Obwohl wir den Anschluss verpasst haben, war es ein unvergesslicher Urlaub. Nothing in it is new grammar: Perfekt, obwohl and a good ending.
By the end you can: tell a holiday story with good and bad moments, in the right order, with als, weil, da, obwohl and feelings.

examples.de: Wir sind nach Tirol gefahren.
examples.en: We went to Tirol.
examples.why: You know this: Perfekt with sein, two verb parts.

examples.de: Obwohl wir den Anschluss verpasst haben, war es ein unvergesslicher Urlaub.
examples.en: Although we missed the connection, it was an unforgettable holiday.
examples.why: New today: the pieces together, with obwohl and a feeling at the end.

cards.more: Imagine you show holiday photos to a friend. If you only say Strand. Regen. Zug. Hotel., the friend learns nothing. If you say what happened first, what went wrong, who helped and how you felt, the same photos become a story. German needs no new grammar for that. It needs order, a few signal words and one feeling at the end. Think of the five photos as five sentences, and the feeling as the caption under the last one.

cards.title: The story skeleton
cards.body: A holiday story has five steps. Say when and where. Start with zuerst or dann. Then comes the problem: plötzlich or leider. Next the rescue: zum Glück. At the end you say how it was. Each step has little signal words. Most of them you know already, so now you only need to put them in the right order.
cards.lead: First we build the frame of every story. These five steps tell you what to say next, and the signal words tell your listener where you are in the story. This frame returns in the next cards.

examples.de: Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug nach Innsbruck gefahren.
examples.en: First we travelled by train to Innsbruck.

examples.de: Plötzlich hat es geregnet.
examples.en: Suddenly it rained.

examples.de: Zum Glück hatte Leon eine Regenjacke.
examples.en: Luckily Leon had a rain jacket.

deeper.text: Signal words can stand in position 1 or after the verb: Plötzlich hat es geregnet. = Es hat plötzlich geregnet. Position 1 gives drama, after the verb it sounds calm. Zum Glück and leider show how you feel about the event, not just when it happened. They are small opinion words: with leider the listener knows the news is bad before the sentence ends.

example.de: Leider ist der Zug ausgefallen.
example.en: Unfortunately the train was cancelled.

cards.more: Picture a road with five signposts. Signpost one says when and where. Two says first. Three has a red warning triangle: plötzlich or leider. Four is a green arrow: zum Glück. Five has a flag: Am Ende war es … You walk along the road one signpost at a time and every signpost gives you a sentence. If you get lost while speaking, go back to the last signpost and continue from there.

rows: Letzten Sommer sind wir nach Tirol gefahren.
Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug gefahren.
Zum Glück hatte Leon eine Regenjacke.
Am Ende war es ein schöner Tag.

steps: 1 When and where? Letzten Sommer …
2 Start: Zuerst … Dann …
3 Problem: Plötzlich … / Leider …
4 Rescue: Zum Glück …
5 End and feeling: Am Ende war es …

cards.title: Things that go wrong
cards.body: On every holiday something goes wrong: a Missgeschick (mishap). Learn the typical ones as short Perfekt sentences. Notice stehlen: an irregular verb with a vowel change, er hat gestohlen. When you do not know who did it, German says jemand. Ben went to the Fundbüro (lost-property office) in Lisbon, and to the Polizei.
cards.lead: Now we collect the typical holiday mishaps. Each one comes as a short Perfekt sentence you can reuse in your own stories, and the table shows the new words in action.

examples.de: Jemand hat Bens Rucksack gestohlen.
examples.en: Someone stole Ben's rucksack.

examples.de: Ben hat einen Sonnenbrand bekommen.
examples.en: Ben got a sunburn.

examples.de: Der Plan ist schiefgegangen.
examples.en: The plan went wrong.

deeper.text: In everyday German people often say klauen instead of stehlen: Jemand hat mein Handy geklaut. It is informal but very common. Natives also like to name the victim in the dative at the start: Mir hat jemand den Rucksack gestohlen. It means the same as Jemand hat meinen Rucksack gestohlen, but it sounds more personal. Use stehlen at the police and in writing, klauen with friends.

example.de: Mir hat jemand das Handy geklaut.
example.en: Someone nicked my phone.

cards.more: Imagine a bad-luck bingo card. Every holiday fills a few squares: sunburn, lost rucksack, storm, a plan that goes wrong. You do not have to learn long sentences. Learn the square and the verb that belongs to it: stehlen, bekommen, erleben, schiefgehen. With the square and the verb you can build the whole sentence in Perfekt, and then you add the person and the place.

cards.title: als and obwohl in the past: one moment, one surprise
cards.body: You know als for one moment in the past: Als wir in Lissabon angekommen sind, war es heiß. In the als clause the Perfekt has both parts at the end, finite verb last. The main clause often uses war or hatte. Add obwohl or weil for a richer story: Obwohl wir müde waren, sind wir in die Altstadt gegangen.
cards.lead: This card repeats als and adds obwohl and weil in past stories. The most important thing is the rhythm: a clause with the verb at the end, then a main clause with the verb first.

examples.de: Als wir in Lissabon angekommen sind, war es heiß.
examples.en: When we arrived in Lisbon, it was hot.

examples.de: Als wir abends zurückgekommen sind, war der Rucksack weg.
examples.en: When we came back in the evening, the rucksack was gone.

examples.de: Obwohl wir müde waren, sind wir in die Altstadt gegangen.
examples.en: Although we were tired, we went into the old town.

deeper.text: Germans tell stories in the Perfekt, but they use the Präteritum for sein, haben and the modal verbs: war, hatte, konnte, wollte. So a native mix sounds like this: Wir sind zum Strand gegangen, aber es war zu voll und wir hatten keinen Platz. Perfekt for the actions, war and hatte for the states around them. You already know both forms.

example.de: Wir sind zum Strand gegangen, aber es war zu voll und wir hatten keinen Platz.
example.en: We went to the beach, but it was too full and we had no space.

cards.more: Think of a camera. als freezes one moment: click, we arrive in Lisbon. Then the main clause tells you what the picture shows: it was hot. So als plus Perfekt is the click, and war or hatte is the photo. For the unexpected, put an obwohl in front of the photo: although we were tired. Three little tools, the same word order every time: first the clause with the verb at the end, then the verb.
steps: 1 als + one moment: Als wir angekommen sind, …
2 In the als clause: participle + sein/haben at the end.
3 Main clause: verb first after the comma: … war es heiß.
4 Extra surprise or reason: obwohl / weil / da, verb at the end.

cards.title: Feelings and judgement: unvergesslich, abenteuerlich, peinlich
cards.body: At the end of a story you say what you think. Three useful words: unvergesslich (unforgettable), abenteuerlich (adventurous) and peinlich (embarrassing). Use them after Es war: Es war peinlich, im Hotel den Schlüssel zu vergessen. This is the zu pattern from the first lessons, now inside a story.
cards.lead: Stories end with an opinion. This card gives you three judgement words and shows how to join them with the zu sentences you already know, so your ending sounds natural and personal.

examples.de: Es war peinlich, im Hotel den Schlüssel zu vergessen.
examples.en: It was embarrassing to forget the key in the hotel.

examples.de: Es war ein unvergesslicher Urlaub, obwohl wir den Anschluss verpasst haben.
examples.en: It was an unforgettable holiday, although we missed the connection.

examples.de: Es war abenteuerlich, in einer Hütte zu schlafen.
examples.en: It was adventurous to sleep in a hut.

deeper.text: Word building helps you remember. Abenteuer (adventure) becomes abenteuerlich with -lich. vergessen becomes vergesslich (forgetful), and with un- it becomes unvergesslich: not forgettable. So the picture is in the word. Be careful with the ending: after ein, the adjective gets -er in the nominative masculine: ein unvergesslicher Urlaub, but Der Urlaub war unvergesslich without ending.

example.de: Der Urlaub war unvergesslich.
example.en: The holiday was unforgettable.

cards.more: Imagine a smiley scale on the wall. Peinlich is the red face. Abenteuerlich is the face with the big eyes. Unvergesslich is the face with the sun. After the story, point to one smiley and say the sentence: Es war … The word you choose tells the listener how to feel about everything you just said. Add a zu part when you want to say what exactly was embarrassing or adventurous.

rows: Es war abenteuerlich, im Zelt zu schlafen.
Es war peinlich, den Schlüssel zu vergessen.

cards.title: Ben's story from Lisbon
cards.body: Read Ben's story. It has everything: a start, a problem, a rescue and an ending. Find the connectors als, weil, obwohl and da. Find zum Glück. Find the moment when the story turns. Notice that the sentences with verbs at the end have a comma, and that the main clause follows with its verb first.
cards.lead: Now a whole story from beginning to end. Read it first for the plot, and then look at the signal words and verb positions you have learned in the last cards.

examples.de: Obwohl Ben einen Sonnenbrand hatte, ist er am Abend in die Altstadt gegangen.
examples.en: Although Ben had a sunburn, he went into the old town in the evening.

examples.de: Als Ben im Café war, hat jemand seinen Rucksack gestohlen.
examples.en: When Ben was in the café, someone stole his rucksack.

examples.de: Da der Reisepass im Rucksack war, ist Ben sofort zur Polizei gegangen.
examples.en: Since his passport was in the rucksack, Ben went to the police at once.

deeper.text: A Fundbüro is an official office. In German-speaking countries, cities and train companies run one, and honest finders bring things there. Owners get them back if they describe the object well. That is why Ben asked the same day: Hat jemand einen Rucksack gebracht? Abroad you cannot always count on that, so the happy ending is even better.

example.de: Hat jemand einen Rucksack gebracht?
example.en: Has someone brought a rucksack?

cards.more: Read the story like a film with five scenes: sun, café, police, phone call, happy end. After the first reading, close the text and tell the five scenes in your own words, even in short sentences. After the second reading, find the five verbs that are at the end of a clause with a conjunction. This is how you notice patterns without a grammar lecture.
steps: Ben und Anna sind im Juni nach Lissabon geflogen.
Ben hat einen Sonnenbrand bekommen, weil er zu lange in der Sonne gelegen hat.
Obwohl Ben einen Sonnenbrand hatte, ist er am Abend in die Altstadt gegangen.
Als er im Café war, hat jemand seinen Rucksack gestohlen.
Da der Reisepass im Rucksack war, ist Ben sofort zur Polizei gegangen. Dort hat er Anzeige erstattet.
Am nächsten Tag hat das Fundbüro angerufen: Jemand hat den Rucksack gefunden und gebracht! Zum Glück war alles noch da.
Ben war erleichtert. Es war ein Missgeschick, aber am Ende war es ein unvergesslicher Urlaub.

cards.title: Your turn: tell your own story
cards.body: Now tell a story of your own, real or invented. Use the five starters below, one sentence each. If something went wrong, say what and how you solved it, and end with a feeling. If somebody tells you about a mishap, answer with the chunk Das kann passieren. (That can happen.)
cards.lead: The last card gives you a frame for speaking and writing. Five starters carry you from the beginning to the end. You only fill in your own details.

examples.de: Letzten Sommer bin ich nach Wien gefahren.
examples.en: Last summer I went to Vienna.

examples.de: Zum Glück hat uns jemand geholfen.
examples.en: Luckily someone helped us.

examples.de: Du hast den Zug verpasst? Das kann passieren.
examples.en: You missed the train? That can happen.

deeper.text: passieren (to happen) uses sein in the Perfekt: Was ist passiert? Das Missgeschick ist am Montag passiert. The English happened does not tell you the helper verb, so learn it as a pair: passiert, ist passiert. A last tip for good stories: put one tiny detail in the first sentence, like the month or the weather. It places the listener in your story at once.

example.de: Was ist passiert?
example.en: What happened?

cards.more: Imagine you meet a friend on the stairs and have two minutes for your story. You cannot say everything. So you pick one problem and one rescue, and you walk along the five signposts: when, first, problem, rescue, end. If the friend asks more, you add one detail. If not, you finish with the feeling. Short stories are easier to tell, and to understand, than long ones.
steps: 1 Letzten Sommer bin ich nach … gefahren. / Im Juli habe ich … gemacht.
2 Zuerst … Dann … Danach …
3 Plötzlich … / Leider …
4 Zum Glück … Als …, …
5 Obwohl …, war es ein … Urlaub.

drills.prompt: Als wir in Lissabon ___, war es heiß.
drills.hint: After als the verbs go to the end. Which helper verb does ankommen use?
drills.explanation: Als wir in Lissabon angekommen sind, war es heiß.

drills.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Als wir angekommen sind, hat es geregnet.
Als wir sind angekommen, hat es geregnet.
Als wir angekommen sind, es hat geregnet.
drills.hint: Verb group at the end of the als clause, then the verb comes first.
drills.explanation: Als wir angekommen sind, hat es geregnet.

drills.prompt: Build: Someone stole Ben's rucksack.
drills.hint: Normal main clause in Perfekt: the participle is last.
drills.explanation: Jemand hat Bens Rucksack gestohlen.

drills.prompt: Ben hat einen Sonnenbrand bekommen, ___ er zu lange in der Sonne gelegen hat.
drills.hint: Is the long time in the sun the reason for the sunburn?
drills.explanation: Ben hat einen Sonnenbrand bekommen, weil er zu lange in der Sonne gelegen hat.

drills.prompt: ___ wir den Anschluss verpasst haben, war es ein schöner Urlaub.
drills.hint: A bad thing, but a good result.
drills.explanation: Obwohl wir den Anschluss verpasst haben, war es ein schöner Urlaub.

drills.prompt: Write in German: Luckily, Leon had a rain jacket. (Start with Zum Glück.)
answers: Zum Glück hatte Leon eine Regenjacke.
Zum Glück hat Leon eine Regenjacke gehabt.
drills.hint: After Zum Glück the verb comes next, then the subject.
drills.explanation: Zum Glück hatte Leon eine Regenjacke.

blind.prompt: Write in German: Although Leon lost his phone, he was happy.
answers: Obwohl Leon sein Handy verloren hat, war er glücklich.
Obwohl Leon sein Handy verloren hat, war Leon glücklich.
Leon war glücklich, obwohl er sein Handy verloren hat.
blind.hint: Perfekt in the obwohl clause: both verb parts go to the end.
blind.explanation: Obwohl Leon sein Handy verloren hat, war er glücklich.

check.prompt: Der Dieb is …
check.hint: Think of stehlen.
check.explanation: der Dieb = the thief.

check.prompt: Jemand hat Bens Rucksack ___. (stehlen)
check.hint: The participle of stehlen is irregular (er stiehlt, er hat …).
check.explanation: Jemand hat Bens Rucksack gestohlen.

check.prompt: Ben ist zum ___ gegangen, denn sein Rucksack war weg.
check.hint: Where do honest finders bring lost things?
check.explanation: Ben ist zum Fundbüro gegangen.

check.prompt: Build: Since the passport was in the rucksack, Ben went to the police at once.
check.hint: Da clause first with the verb at its end, then the verb of the main clause.
check.explanation: Da der Reisepass im Rucksack war, ist Ben sofort zur Polizei gegangen.

check.prompt: Es war peinlich, im Hotel den Schlüssel ___ vergessen.
check.hint: A zu sentence after the comma: zu stands right before the verb.
check.explanation: Es war peinlich, im Hotel den Schlüssel zu vergessen.

check.prompt: Which sentence has the right word order?
options: Zum Glück jemand hat uns geholfen.
Zum Glück hat uns jemand geholfen.
Zum Glück uns hat jemand geholfen.
check.hint: After Zum Glück the verb is second.
check.explanation: Zum Glück hat uns jemand geholfen.

check.prompt: Der Plan ___ schiefgegangen.
check.hint: schiefgehen is a verb of change. Which helper verb belongs to it in the Perfekt?
check.explanation: Der Plan ist schiefgegangen.

check.prompt: Wir haben den Zug verpasst, ___ sind wir mit dem Bus gefahren.
check.hint: A result, and the verb comes right after the word.
check.explanation: Wir haben den Zug verpasst, deshalb sind wir mit dem Bus gefahren.

check.prompt: Das Unwetter is …
check.hint: Un- means bad, Wetter is weather.
check.explanation: das Unwetter = severe weather, a storm.

check.prompt: Write in German: That can happen.
check.hint: A chunk, learn it as a whole.
check.explanation: Das kann passieren.

examples.en: That was a small mishap.

examples.de: Im Urlaub passiert immer ein Missgeschick.
examples.en: On holiday there is always a mishap.

examples.de: Wir sind zum Fundbüro gegangen.
examples.en: We went to the lost-property office.

examples.de: Ben hat einen Sonnenbrand bekommen.

examples.de: Ein Sonnenbrand tut weh.
examples.en: A sunburn hurts.

examples.de: Wir haben ein Unwetter erlebt.
examples.en: We experienced a storm.

examples.de: Nach dem Unwetter war der Himmel klar.
examples.en: After the storm the sky was clear.

examples.de: Der Plan ist schiefgegangen.
examples.en: The plan went wrong.

examples.de: Hoffentlich geht nichts schief!
examples.en: Hopefully nothing goes wrong!

examples.de: Es war ein unvergesslicher Urlaub.
examples.en: It was an unforgettable holiday.

examples.de: Der Abend war unvergesslich.
examples.en: The evening was unforgettable.

examples.de: Die Reise war abenteuerlich.
examples.en: The journey was adventurous.

examples.de: Es war abenteuerlich, im Zelt zu schlafen.
examples.en: It was adventurous to sleep in a tent.

examples.de: Das ist mir peinlich.
examples.en: That is embarrassing for me.

examples.en: It was embarrassing to forget the key.

examples.de: Ben hat bei der Polizei Anzeige erstattet.
examples.en: Ben made a report to the police.

examples.de: Die Anzeige dauert zehn Minuten.
examples.en: The report takes ten minutes.

examples.de: Ben ist zur Polizei gegangen.
examples.en: Ben went to the police.

examples.de: Die Polizei hilft.
examples.en: The police help.

examples.de: Das ist ein Notfall!
examples.en: That is an emergency!

examples.de: Im Notfall rufe ich die 112 an.
examples.en: In an emergency I call 112.

examples.de: Du hast den Zug verpasst? Das kann passieren.
examples.en: You missed the train? That can happen.

examples.en: That can happen, do not worry.

examples.de: Zum Glück war alles noch da.

prompts: Tell a short story about a holiday mishap. Use zuerst, plötzlich and zum Glück.
Say what happened when you arrived somewhere. Use als.
Say how a trip was, and why it was good although something went wrong. Use obwohl.
examples: Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug gefahren. Plötzlich ist der Zug ausgefallen. Zum Glück hat uns jemand geholfen.
Als wir in Wien angekommen sind, hat es geregnet. Wir sind in ein Café gegangen.
Obwohl wir den Bus verpasst haben, war es ein schöner Tag. Es war abenteuerlich.

retrieval.prompt: Mira geht weiter, obwohl sie eine Blase ___. (haben)
retrieval.hint: Verb at the end, sie form.
retrieval.explanation: Mira geht weiter, obwohl sie eine Blase hat.

retrieval.prompt: Write in German: I have no time to call you.
answers: Ich habe keine Zeit, dich anzurufen.
retrieval.hint: keine Zeit haben + zu. anrufen is separable.
retrieval.explanation: Ich habe keine Zeit, dich anzurufen.

retrieval.prompt: Da es regnet, ___ Mira in der Hütte. (bleiben)
retrieval.hint: The verb comes right after the comma and fits Mira.
retrieval.explanation: Da es regnet, bleibt Mira in der Hütte.

retrieval.prompt: Write in German: It is nice to sleep in a tent.
answers: Es ist schön, im Zelt zu schlafen.
retrieval.hint: Es ist + adjective, comma, zu before the verb.
retrieval.explanation: Es ist schön, im Zelt zu schlafen.

lessons.title: Achtung an Gleis 12!: understanding announcements, and n, ng, nk
lessons.goal: Understand station, train and airport announcements by listening for the five key facts, use da and obwohl in them, and pronounce n, ng and nk.

grammar.topic: Announcements, da and obwohl, pronunciation of n, ng, nk
grammar.point: Listen for five facts: which train or flight, where, when, the problem, what to do. Announcements give reasons with da (verb at the end of the da clause, then the verb first): Da es eine Störung gibt, fährt der Zug später ab. Pronunciation: ng is one sound [ŋ] with no g, nk is [ŋk], and -ung is always [ʊŋ].
grammar.oneLine: Da es eine Störung gibt, fährt der Zug später ab.

mistake.why: ng is one sound, like in English sing, never n + g. The ending -ung is always [ʊŋ]: Achtung, Wohnung.

terms.meaning: a spoken message over a loudspeaker: die Durchsage or die Ansage
two words that differ in only one sound, like dann and Dank

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Der Zug hat Verspätung' to a whole announcement
cards.body: Mira and Leon stand on a platform and a loudspeaker crackles. Fast German, many numbers, a long sentence. You do not need to understand every word. You need the key facts: which train, which platform, when, what is wrong and what to do. Today you learn to listen for exactly these.
steps: You already know: Der Zug fährt von Gleis 7. Der Zug hat Verspätung.
New today: Der ICE nach München hat voraussichtlich 20 Minuten Verspätung. Da es eine Störung gibt, … The sentences are longer, but the key words are the same.
By the end you can: understand station, train and airport announcements by listening for key words, and say n, ng and nk correctly.

examples.de: Der Zug hat Verspätung.
examples.en: The train has a delay.
examples.why: You know this: a short announcement.

examples.de: Der ICE nach München hat voraussichtlich 20 Minuten Verspätung.
examples.en: The ICE to Munich is expected to be 20 minutes late.
examples.why: New today: the same sentence with one new word and more detail.

cards.more: Think of the station as a quiz show. The loudspeaker asks no questions, but it answers five of them very fast, and you only have to catch the answers. You do not translate. You wait for the number, the platform, the time and the problem. Real travellers do the same, even in their own language, because station announcements are long and noisy. Five facts are your whole job, and the rest is background noise.

cards.title: Five questions for every announcement
cards.body: Listen with five questions in your head. Which train or flight? Where: which Gleis or Gate? When? What is the problem, the reason? What should I do? Listen twice in your mind: first only for the train and the platform, then only for the problem and the action. Everything else can stay unclear.
cards.lead: Before we learn the typical phrases, here is the strategy that makes every announcement easier. It is the same for trains, buses and planes, and it works even when you miss half the words.

examples.de: Der ICE nach München fährt von Gleis 12 ab.
examples.en: The ICE to Munich leaves from platform 12.

examples.de: Der Zug hat voraussichtlich 20 Minuten Verspätung.
examples.en: The train has an expected delay of 20 minutes.

examples.de: Ihr Anschlusszug wartet.
examples.en: Your connecting train is waiting.

deeper.text: Times in announcements are said with the 24-hour clock: Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr fünfunddreißig ab means 2:35 pm. Numbers come fast, so listen for the first digit and the last digit. If you hear fünfzehn and fünfzig, be careful: they sound alike. The key is the sound at the end: -zehn or -zig. Check the number on the display.

example.de: Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr fünfunddreißig ab.
example.en: The train leaves at 14:35.

cards.more: Imagine you are a detective at the station and have five questions on a card. You do not need the whole story. Which train is the suspect? Where does it stand? When does it move? What is the problem? What should you do? Tick every question you can answer. If four boxes are ticked, you understood the announcement. A missing box tells you where to listen harder the next time.
steps: 1 Which train or flight? (Zug nach …, Flug …)
2 Where? (Gleis, Gate, Haltestelle)
3 When? (um … Uhr, in … Minuten)
4 What is the problem? (Verspätung, Störung, fällt aus)
5 What should I do? (umsteigen, warten, einsteigen)

cards.title: Typical announcement pieces
cards.body: Announcements are built from small pieces that come back again and again. Learn the pieces as chunks, and you will recognise them even when the rest is unclear. Here are the most common ones at the station and on board. Notice the typical words Achtung, voraussichtlich, Ersatzverkehr and Ausstieg.
cards.lead: Now we collect the building blocks of announcements. You will not say them yourself, you only recognise them. They appear in almost every German train station, so they are very good value for your ears.

examples.de: Achtung an Gleis 12!
examples.en: Attention at platform 12!

examples.de: Der Zug fällt heute aus.
examples.en: The train is cancelled today.

examples.de: Nächster Halt: Innsbruck.
examples.en: Next stop: Innsbruck.

deeper.text: Fahrtrichtung means the direction the train is travelling. Ausstieg in Fahrtrichtung rechts means: the doors open on the right side as seen in the direction of travel, not as seen when you look at the door. If you sit with your back to the engine, right is your left. Look at where the front of the train is, then decide.

example.de: Ausstieg in Fahrtrichtung rechts.
example.en: Exit on the right in the direction of travel.

cards.more: Think of puzzle pieces. A whole announcement is a puzzle with only six or seven different pieces: Achtung, Verspätung, fällt aus, Ersatzverkehr, Anschlusszug wartet, Grund dafür ist and Nächster Halt. If you know the pieces, you do not need the whole picture. You see two or three pieces and you know what the picture is. This is why good listeners understand announcements without knowing all the words.

rows: be careful, a train is arriving
is expected to be … minutes late
Nächster Halt: … / Ausstieg in Fahrtrichtung rechts
next stop … / exit on the right (direction of travel)

cards.title: At the airport: formal words you only recognise
cards.body: At the airport you hear Abflug, Gate, Bordkarte and Gepäckausgabe. The language is more formal than in everyday life. Der Abflug verzögert sich means: the flight is delayed. Bitte begeben Sie sich zu Gate B12 means: please go to Gate B12. Recognise these sentences, you do not have to say them.
cards.lead: Airport announcements use words that nobody says in a normal conversation. This card shows the most important ones, so you can understand them and then act. You only need to recognise them.

examples.de: Der Abflug verzögert sich um 30 Minuten.
examples.en: The flight is delayed by 30 minutes.

examples.de: Bitte halten Sie Ihre Bordkarte bereit.
examples.en: Please have your boarding pass ready.

deeper.text: Announcements use formal verbs that you only need to recognise. sich begeben is a formal way to say gehen. verkehren is a formal word for fahren: Der Zug verkehrt nicht means: the train does not run. You will never need to say these words yourself, but you will hear them in every big station. If you hear them, think: go, or run.

example.de: Der Zug verkehrt heute nicht.
example.en: The train does not run today.

cards.more: Imagine a translator who turns announcements into friendly language. Bitte begeben Sie sich zu Gate B12 becomes: Bitte gehen Sie zu Gate B12. Der Abflug verzögert sich becomes: Der Flug startet später. The translator takes the formal verb away and keeps the nouns and the numbers. You can do this too: ignore the stiff verb and listen for the nouns: Gate, Bordkarte, Gepäckausgabe. Gate B12 and the number are what you act on.

cards.title: da in announcements: the reason comes first
cards.body: You know da from lesson five: a reason that everybody can see, usually at the start, verb at the end. Announcements love da, because the reason is a fact that is already known: Da der Zug Verspätung hat, erreichen Sie Ihren Anschlusszug nicht. After the da clause the main clause starts with its verb.
cards.lead: Here the new grammar of the chapter meets the station. Announcements use da to give a reason, and you already know how it works: verb at the end, then verb first. We look at three typical examples.

examples.de: Da es eine Störung gibt, fährt der Zug später ab.
examples.en: Since there is a disruption, the train leaves later.

examples.de: Da der ICE Verspätung hat, wartet der Anschlusszug.
examples.en: Since the train is delayed, the connecting train is waiting.

examples.de: Da ein Zug ausgefallen ist, fährt ein Bus.
examples.en: Since a train has been cancelled, a bus is running.

deeper.text: Announcements rarely use weil. They state the reason with da, or they name it afterwards with a noun: Grund dafür ist eine Störung. You hear it as two sentences, one for the problem and one for the reason. The da form is more formal and more written, and weil is for chatting. You will use da when you write a polite email or a message to a hotel.

example.de: Grund dafür ist eine Störung.
example.en: The reason for this is a disruption.

cards.more: Imagine a sign on the platform. The sign is already there when you arrive. It says: Störung. Now the loudspeaker says da, which means: since you can see the sign. Da is the word for facts the listener already knows or can see. Weil is the word for a fresh answer to a question. In announcements, the reason is part of the situation, so da is the natural word.
steps: 1 Start with Da + reason: Da es eine Störung gibt,
2 The verb of the reason goes last: gibt,
3 Main clause: verb first: fährt der Zug später ab.

cards.title: n, ng, nk: say them right
cards.body: Three sounds look alike, but sound different. n is the normal n: dann, Bahn. ng is one single sound, [ŋ], like in the English word sing: Achtung, singen, lang. There is no g to hear. nk is the same sound plus a k: Dank, Bank, krank. The ending -ung is always [ʊŋ].
cards.lead: This card trains your ears and your mouth on three small sounds that appear in many announcements. Short pairs of words help you hear the difference.

examples.de: Achtung, der Zug fährt ein!
examples.en: Attention, the train is arriving!

examples.de: Danke für die Auskunft, Herr Ali.
examples.en: Thank you for the information, Mr Ali.

examples.de: Die Bank ist lang.
examples.en: The bench is long.

deeper.text: A trap for English speakers: in English finger has [ŋ] plus a hard g. In German Finger has only [ŋ], with no g at all, just like Sänger or Hunger. The exception comes where two word parts meet: in Eingang (ein + Gang) you hear an n and then a hard g. Say Ein-gang, in two beats.

example.de: Der Eingang ist links.
example.en: The entrance is on the left.

cards.more: Try this with your tongue. Say the English word sing and stop before the end. Your tongue is at the back of your mouth, and the sound goes through the nose. That is the German ng. For n, put your tongue at the front, behind your top teeth. For nk, say ng, then close the back of the mouth for a k. Do the three positions in a mirror: front, back, back and closed.
steps: n: tongue at the front: Bahn, nein, dann.
ng: one sound, no g: Achtung, singen, lang, Wohnung.
nk: ng + k: danke, Bank, krank, Getränk.
-ung at the end is always [ʊŋ].

cards.title: On the platform in München: Mira and Leon
cards.body: Read the dialogue. Mira and Leon wait on platform 11 in München Hbf. The loudspeaker says that their train to Innsbruck is 25 minutes late. Find the five answers: which train, where, how long, why, what to do. Notice two chunks: Wir bitten um Verständnis (we ask for your understanding) and Halb so schlimm.
cards.lead: The last card puts everything together: the five questions, da, the typical pieces and a real decision. Read the announcement first, then the reaction, and find where Mira and Leon use obwohl and weil.

examples.de: Der Zug nach Innsbruck hat voraussichtlich 25 Minuten Verspätung.
examples.en: The train to Innsbruck is expected to be 25 minutes late.

examples.de: Da es eine Störung gibt, wissen sie nicht genau, wann wir abfahren.
examples.en: Since there is a disruption, they do not know exactly when we leave.

examples.de: Obwohl der Zug später kommt, schaffen wir es bestimmt.
examples.en: Although the train comes later, we will certainly make it.

deeper.text: Wir bitten um Verständnis is the polite way of saying sorry for the inconvenience. The railway company does not say Entschuldigung, it asks for understanding, in a formal and calm way. You will hear this at every station in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. You only need to recognise it. A good answer from a traveller, if you want to say something, is Halb so schlimm, which you know.

example.de: Wir bitten um Verständnis.
example.en: We ask for your understanding.

cards.more: Read the dialogue twice. The first time, ignore the grammar and tick the five questions: which train, where, how long, why, what now. The second time, underline the verbs at the end of da, weil and obwohl clauses. Then cover the German and try to retell the situation in your own words. Three sentences are enough: the train is late, there is a disruption, they decide to wait.
steps: Durchsage: Achtung an Gleis 11! Der Zug nach Innsbruck hat voraussichtlich 25 Minuten Verspätung. Grund dafür ist eine Störung. Wir bitten um Verständnis.
Leon: Hast du das verstanden? Wie viel Verspätung hat der Zug?
Mira: Fünfundzwanzig Minuten. Da es eine Störung gibt, wissen sie nicht genau, wann wir abfahren.
Leon: Dann verpassen wir vielleicht unseren Bus in Innsbruck.
Mira: Obwohl der Zug später kommt, schaffen wir es bestimmt. Der Bus fährt erst um 19 Uhr.
Leon: Halb so schlimm. Dann essen wir hier noch etwas.
Mira: Gute Idee. Weil wir warten müssen, nehmen wir eine Brezel.
Leon: Und wir bleiben ruhig. Wir schaffen das!

lessons.title: Ein Sommer auf der Alm: working on an alpine pasture
lessons.goal: Understand and talk about life and work on an Alm, say why someone does it and what is hard about it, using da, weil, obwohl and zu.

grammar.topic: Alm culture; da, weil, obwohl and zu in use
grammar.point: No new grammar today: you use what you know. Reasons with weil or da (verb at the end), contrasts with obwohl (verb at the end), and zu + infinitive after Lust haben or Es ist schwer. The Alm always takes auf: auf der Alm (where?), auf die Alm (where to?).
grammar.oneLine: Obwohl die Arbeit hart ist, möchte Mira den Sommer auf der Alm verbringen.

mistake.why: An Alm is an open surface on a mountain, so German uses auf, like auf dem Berg or auf dem Land: auf der Alm (where?), auf die Alm (where to?).

terms.meaning: a high summer pasture in the Alps with a hut, where cows spend the summer
the day in autumn when the cows walk back down to the valley
the usual greeting in Austria and Bavaria, like Guten Tag

cards.title: Before we start: from a hiking holiday to a working holiday on the Alm
cards.body: Mira and Leon came to Tirol for a hiking week. Now Mira has a new plan: friends of her aunt have an Alm, and she can help there for two weeks. Today you learn what an Alm is and what people do there, and you use everything from this chapter: zu, weil, da and obwohl.
steps: You already know: Mira wandert in den Bergen. Es ist anstrengend, früh aufzustehen.
New today: life on an Alm, the words for cows, milk and cheese, and the little word auf: auf der Alm.
By the end you can: describe a day on an Alm, say why people work there and what is hard, and discuss pros and cons.

examples.de: Es ist anstrengend, früh aufzustehen.
examples.en: It is tiring to get up early.
examples.why: You know this: Es ist + adjective + zu (lesson 3).

examples.de: Obwohl die Arbeit hart ist, möchte Mira den Sommer auf der Alm verbringen.
examples.en: Although the work is hard, Mira wants to spend the summer on the Alm.
examples.why: New today: the same obwohl, now about a new world, the Alm.

cards.more: Picture two postcards from Tirol. The first one shows Mira with a rucksack on a summit: that is a holiday, she walks and then she rests. The second one shows Mira at five in the morning next to a cow with a bucket: that is a working holiday. Same mountains, a very different life. Today you look at the second postcard. You will not learn new grammar rules; you will use your weil, da, obwohl and zu to talk about a real Alpine tradition.

cards.title: What is an Alm?
cards.body: An Alm is a summer pasture high in the Alps, with a small hut and a stable. Alms exist in Austria, Bavaria and Switzerland. In early summer, about June, the cows go up. Until September they eat fresh grass there. A Sennerin or a Senner looks after them, milks them and makes cheese.
cards.lead: Before Mira can tell us about her summer, we need the basics. This card answers four questions about the Alm: where it is, when people go, who works there and what they do.

examples.de: Die Alm liegt hoch in den Bergen.
examples.en: The Alm lies high up in the mountains.

examples.de: Im Juni gehen die Kühe auf die Alm.
examples.en: In June the cows go up to the Alm.

examples.de: Die Sennerin melkt die Kühe und macht Käse.
examples.en: The dairywoman milks the cows and makes cheese.

rows: in den Alpen: Österreich, Bayern, Schweiz
im Sommer, ungefähr Juni bis September
die Kühe hüten, melken, Käse machen

deeper.text: Why do farmers take the cows so high? Down in the valley, the meadows are needed for hay, the dry grass the cows eat in winter. So in summer the animals eat on the mountain, and the valley grass can grow. Many people also say that milk and cheese from the Alm taste better, because the cows eat mountain herbs. That is why Almkäse is a famous speciality.

example.de: Im Sommer fressen die Kühe auf der Alm, und im Tal wächst das Gras für den Winter.
example.en: In summer the cows eat on the Alm, and in the valley the grass grows for the winter.

cards.more: Think of the Alm as a summer camp for cows. Every year, when school ends for children, the cows also leave home: they walk from the farm in the valley up the mountain. Up there they have fresh grass, cool air and a lot of space. A Sennerin is like the camp leader: she looks after them all summer. When autumn comes and it gets cold, camp is over and everybody walks back down. English has no single word for this, so English texts often just say Alm.

cards.title: A day on the Alm
cards.body: A day on the Alm starts very early. At five o'clock the Sennerin gets up and milks the cows. Then she drives them to the pasture. In the morning she makes cheese and butter. In the afternoon she cleans the stable. In the evening she milks again, and then it is quiet.
cards.lead: Now you know what an Alm is. This card follows one day from five in the morning to the evening, with separable verbs like aufstehen and the time at the start of the sentence.
steps: 5 Uhr: Die Sennerin steht auf und melkt die Kühe.
7 Uhr: Sie treibt die Kühe auf die Weide.
Vormittag: Sie macht Käse und Butter.
Nachmittag: Sie putzt den Stall.
Abend: Sie melkt noch einmal. Dann ist Ruhe.

examples.de: Um fünf Uhr steht Mira auf.
examples.en: At five o'clock Mira gets up.

examples.de: Danach treibt sie die Kühe auf die Weide.
examples.en: After that she drives the cows to the pasture.

examples.de: Am Nachmittag putzt sie den Stall.
examples.en: In the afternoon she cleans the stable.

deeper.text: Cows must be milked twice a day, every day, also on Sundays and in bad weather. So on an Alm there is no free weekend. That is a big difference from a normal summer job. People also say: Die Kühe geben Milch (the cows give milk). The word for an animal eating is fressen, not essen: Die Kühe fressen Gras. Use essen only for people.

example.de: Die Kühe fressen Gras und geben viel Milch.
example.en: The cows eat grass and give a lot of milk.

cards.more: Imagine a clock with only five stops. At five the alarm rings and the first job waits: milking. At seven the cows walk out to the grass. In the late morning the kitchen smells of warm milk, because the cheese is made. In the afternoon comes the dirty job, the stable. In the evening, milking again, and then silence. Notice how each sentence starts with the time and the verb comes second: Um fünf Uhr steht sie auf. That is the rhythm of German stories.

cards.title: Why people do it
cards.body: The work is hard and the pay is low. So why do people spend a summer on an Alm? They give reasons with weil and da, and they admit the problems with obwohl. Many also say what they feel like doing with Lust haben, … zu. All these verbs go to the end.
cards.lead: After the facts come the reasons. Here you use weil, da and obwohl, which you already know, to explain why someone chooses a hard summer on the mountain.

rows: Da es dort keinen Stress gibt, fühlen sich viele wohl.
Mira geht auf die Alm, weil sie die Natur liebt.
Obwohl man kaum Geld verdient, kommen viele jedes Jahr.
Viele haben Lust, einmal ohne Handy zu leben.

examples.de: Da es dort keinen Stress gibt, fühlen sich viele wohl.
examples.en: Since there is no stress there, many feel good.

examples.de: Viele haben Lust, einmal ohne Handy zu leben.
examples.en: Many feel like living without a mobile phone for once.

examples.de: Obwohl man kaum Geld verdient, kommen viele jedes Jahr wieder.
examples.en: Although you hardly earn any money, many come back every year.

deeper.text: Who works on an Alm today? Not only farmers. Students, teachers and office workers from cities also apply for a summer as helpers, often for a few weeks. There are even courses where you can learn the work first. Many say they want a break from the screen. A typical sentence you hear: Ich habe gemerkt, wie wenig man braucht (I noticed how little you need).

example.de: Ich habe gemerkt, wie wenig man braucht.
example.en: I noticed how little you need.

cards.more: Think of a scale with two sides. On the heavy side: early mornings, rain, dirty boots, very little money. On the light side: quiet, stars, fresh cheese, no phone. With weil and da you put things on the good side: Ich gehe hin, weil es ruhig ist. With obwohl you name the heavy side and still say yes: Obwohl ich wenig verdiene, gehe ich hin. When obwohl wins, the decision is strong, because the person knows the problem and goes anyway.

cards.title: Almabtrieb: the cows come home
cards.body: In September or October the summer on the Alm ends. The cows walk down to the valley. This is the Almabtrieb. Often the cows wear flowers and big bells, and the village celebrates with music and food. Many tourists come to watch. The cows go up: auf die Alm. They come down: ins Tal.
cards.lead: Every Alm summer has an end. This card shows the big autumn festival when the cows come down, and why they are sometimes decorated and sometimes not.

examples.de: Im September kommen die Kühe ins Tal.
examples.en: In September the cows come down to the valley.

examples.de: Die Bauern schmücken die Kühe mit Blumen und Glocken.
examples.en: The farmers decorate the cows with flowers and bells.

examples.de: Das ganze Dorf feiert den Almabtrieb.
examples.en: The whole village celebrates the Almabtrieb.

deeper.text: Austria and Bavaria say die Alm; in Switzerland people say die Alp, and the men and women who work there are often called Älpler. The decoration has a meaning: traditionally the cows wear flowers only if the summer went well and no animal died and nobody was badly hurt on the Alm. If something bad happened, the cows come down without decoration. In Austria and Bavaria people greet you with Grüß Gott!

example.de: Grüß Gott! Kommen Sie zum Almabtrieb?
example.en: Hello! Are you coming to the Almabtrieb?

cards.more: Picture a parade where the stars are cows. They walk slowly down the road, the big bells ring, and the first cow has a huge crown of flowers. People stand at the side and take photos. It is a bit like a homecoming party after a long trip: everybody is happy that the animals are back. For your German, remember the two directions. Going up is auf die Alm. Coming down is ins Tal. And staying there all summer is auf der Alm.

cards.title: A message from the Alm
cards.body: Read Mira's message to the WG. Find what she does every day, what she likes and what is difficult. Look for two new words: einsam (lonely) and abgelegen (remote). And find the sentence about electricity: is there none at all, or only a little?
cards.lead: Now Mira writes herself. Her message to the WG uses the Alm words from this lesson together with obwohl, da and zu, so you can see them in a real text.

examples.de: Hallo zusammen, ich bin jetzt seit drei Tagen auf der Alm!
examples.en: Hi everyone, I have been on the Alm for three days now!

steps: Hallo zusammen, ich bin jetzt seit drei Tagen auf der Alm!
Jeden Morgen um fünf melke ich mit der Sennerin die Kühe. Ihre Glocken höre ich die ganze Nacht.
Da die Hütte sehr abgelegen ist, gibt es nur wenig Strom. Mein Handy lade ich nur abends.
Obwohl es manchmal einsam ist, finde ich es toll, hier zu sein. Der Sternenhimmel ist unglaublich!

Liebe Grüße aus Tirol
Mira

deeper.text: Many Alm huts are far from the next road and have no normal power line. They get electricity from a small solar panel or a little water power station, so there is enough for light and a fridge, but not for much more. That is why Mira charges her phone only in the evening. The word abgelegen comes from liegen: something that lies far away from everything.

example.de: Die Hütte hat eine kleine Solaranlage.
example.en: The hut has a small solar power system.

cards.more: Read the message like a detective with three questions. First: what does Mira do? She milks at five with the Sennerin. Second: what is good? The stars, the bells, the feeling of being there. Third: what is hard? The hut is far away, there is only a little electricity, and sometimes she feels alone. Now look at the grammar inside: the da sentence gives a known reason, and the obwohl sentence names a problem but ends with a yes.

cards.title: Leon visits: pros and cons
cards.body: Leon comes up for a day. He wants to become a cook, so he loves the fresh cheese. Read the dialogue and find one pro and one con for each of them. Listen for zu after a noun or adjective, da with a known reason and obwohl with a contrast.
cards.lead: To finish, two friends discuss the Alm. Leon sees the cheese, Mira sees the work. Their dialogue mixes all the patterns of the chapter, so read it twice.
steps: Leon: Grüß Gott, Mira! Wow, die Aussicht ist ja wunderschön!
Mira: Hallo Leon! Komm rein, ich habe gerade Käse gemacht.
Leon: Dieser Käse ist fantastisch! Ich habe Lust, hier kochen zu lernen.
Mira: Das glaube ich dir. Aber es ist anstrengend, jeden Tag um fünf aufzustehen.
Leon: Und trotzdem bist du glücklich, oder?
Mira: Ja. Obwohl ich kaum Geld verdiene, möchte ich nächstes Jahr wiederkommen.
Leon: Da die Hütte so abgelegen ist, hast du bestimmt keinen Stress.
Mira: Genau. Nur die Kühe machen manchmal Stress!

examples.de: Ich habe Lust, hier kochen zu lernen.
examples.en: I feel like learning to cook here.

examples.de: Obwohl ich kaum Geld verdiene, möchte ich nächstes Jahr wiederkommen.
examples.en: Although I hardly earn any money, I would like to come back next year.

examples.de: Da die Hütte so abgelegen ist, hast du bestimmt keinen Stress.
examples.en: Since the hut is so remote, you surely have no stress.

deeper.text: Look at Ich habe Lust, hier kochen zu lernen. Two infinitives stand at the end: kochen and lernen. Only the last one, lernen, gets zu, because lernen belongs to Lust. kochen belongs to lernen, and after lernen you use no zu, like after a modal verb. The same works with schwimmen lernen and Ski fahren lernen: Es ist nie zu spät, schwimmen zu lernen.

example.de: Es ist nie zu spät, schwimmen zu lernen.
example.en: It is never too late to learn to swim.

cards.more: Think of the dialogue as a game of ping pong. Leon hits a pro: the view, the cheese. Mira hits back a con: getting up at five. Leon tries again: you are happy anyway. Mira answers with obwohl, the best shot of the game, because it holds a con and a pro in one sentence. At the end Leon serves a da sentence, and Mira closes with a joke. When you discuss pros and cons in German, do the same: answer a pro with a con.
